pr.title: fix: draft relocated base objects at previously assigned indices in array-methods plugin
pr.body:
## Summary

With `enableArrayMethods()`, a base object that an earlier call relocated onto an index that already has an `assigned_` entry comes back from the get trap undrafted. Writing to it mutates the base state, and throws on a frozen base.

`isRelocatedBaseRef` in `src/core/proxy.ts` (added in #1255) returns false when `state.assigned_?.get(prop)` is set. `push`, `unshift`, `splice` and index writes all put indices into `assigned_`, and those entries stay there. Once the elements are reordered they describe an index, not the value that now sits there, so the guard skips base objects it should draft.

```ts
const base = {items: [{id: "a", n: 1}, {id: "b", n: 2}, {id: "c", n: 3}]}
produce(base, d => {
  d.items.push({id: "d", n: 4})
  d.items.reverse()
  d.items[3].n = 100 // items[3] is the base object `a`, returned raw
})
// base.items[0].n === 100
```

Without the plugin the base is untouched. With a frozen base this throws `TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'n'`. The same thing happens with `push` + `unshift`, `unshift` + `reverse`, an index write + `sort`, and `splice` + `reverse`. A more everyday shape:

```ts
produce(frozenBase, d => {
  d.items.push(newItem)
  d.items.sort((a, b) => a.id - b.id)
  d.items.filter(i => i.id === 3)[0].v = 5 // throws; find() and slice() too
})
```

## Fix

Drop the `assigned_` check from `isRelocatedBaseRef`. `baseRefs_` (a snapshot of the base elements, taken when the array is first reordered) already identifies a relocated base object, and a user-provided object is never in it, so it is still returned as-is. Already-drafted values are still skipped by the `value[DRAFT_STATE]` check. The positional check next to it (`value === base_[prop]`) already drafts a base object that is assigned back to its own index, so this is consistent with that.

## Test plan

Added to `__tests__/base.js` under "mutating array methods" (so they run in every config, including with the plugin):

- five push/unshift/index write/splice + reverse/sort/unshift recipes, each checked for "base is not mutated" and "works on a frozen base"
- `find()`, `filter()` and `slice()` after `push()` + `sort()` return drafts on a frozen base
- guard: a newly assigned object is still returned undrafted, while the relocated base objects are drafted
- guard: patches and inverse patches round-trip for a push/unshift + reverse case

With only the `proxy.ts` change reverted, 12 of the new tests fail (base mutated / `Cannot assign to read only property`), and they pass with the fix. The existing reverse/sort tests from #1255 still pass.

Full `vitest run`: 23 files, 3962 passed, 8 skipped. `tsup` build + `vitest run --config vitest.config.build.ts` also passes. I did not run `yarn test:flow`.

I also fuzzed 6000 random sequences of push/unshift/splice/index write/pop/shift/reverse/sort followed by a nested write, comparing plugin on vs. off. Before: 184 cases mutated the base and 184 threw on a frozen base. After: none, and the resulting state matches the plugin-off result in every case.

pr.title: fix: resolve the splice start index against the pre-splice length in array-methods plugin
pr.body:
## Summary

`splice` in the array-methods plugin resolves the start index against the array length after the splice has already run (`src/plugins/arrayMethods.ts`, the `normalizeSliceIndex(args[0] ?? 0, state.copy_!.length)` call that feeds `handleInsertedValues`). For a negative start or a start past the end, the post-splice length gives a different index than the native method used. The inserted values are then registered (`assigned_` + `handleCrossReference`) at the wrong index, so a value that contains a draft is never replaced during finalization and ends up pointing at a revoked proxy:

```ts
const base = {items: [{a: 1}, {a: 2}, {a: 3}]}
produce(base, draft => {
  draft.items.splice(-2, 0, {copy: draft.items[0]})
})
// TypeError: Cannot perform 'get' on a proxy that has been revoked
```

Without the plugin this gives `[{a:1},{copy:{a:1}},{a:2},{a:3}]`. The same happens for `splice(-1, ...)`, `splice(100, ...)`, and for `splice(-1, 0, {...draft.items[0]})` when the item has nested objects (a "duplicate this item" recipe). In-range positive starts are fine, since they don't depend on the length.

## Fix

Capture `state.copy_.length` right before the native `splice` call and use it for the start index. `normalizeSliceIndex` itself is untouched, so this doesn't overlap with #1313 (which changes how fractional indices are normalized).

## Test plan

Added `splice() inserting values that contain drafts` to `__tests__/base.js` (runs in every config, so it also pins the plugin-off behavior). It covers start `-2`, `-1`, `100`, an in-range start (`1`) as a guard, a negative start with a `deleteCount`, and the `{...draft.items[0]}` duplicate case. The first four also check that the base is untouched and that patches and inverse patches round-trip.

With only the `arrayMethods.ts` change reverted, 4 of the new tests fail with `Cannot perform 'has' on a proxy that has been revoked`, and they pass with the fix.

Full `vitest run`: 23 files, 3890 passed, 8 skipped. `tsup` build + `vitest run --config vitest.config.build.ts` also passes. I did not run `yarn test:flow`.

pr.title: fix: skip nested patches for children of shifted or reordered arrays

gold_patch:
diff --git a/src/plugins/patches.ts b/src/plugins/patches.ts
index 08c7d0f..4db8c3a 100644
--- a/src/plugins/patches.ts
+++ b/src/plugins/patches.ts
@@ -90,6 +90,18 @@ export function enablePatches() {
 				return null // Key deleted
 			}
 
+			// Once an array's elements have been shifted or reordered, a child's index
+			// no longer matches its position in the base. The array generates a patch
+			// for every index that changed (carrying the finalized child), so a nested
+			// patch at the child's new index is redundant and, for an index past the
+			// base length, points at a path that does not exist yet when it is applied.
+			if (
+				state.parent_!.type_ === ArchType.Array &&
+				(state.parent_ as ProxyArrayState).allIndicesReassigned_
+			) {
+				return null
+			}
+
 			// Step 5: Add key to path
 			path.push(key)
 		}

pr.title: fix: avoid endless iteration in current Set snapshots
pr.body:
`current()` never returns for a modified Set containing an ordinary object:

```js
enableMapSet()
produce(new Set([{count: 0}]), draft => {
  draft.values().next().value.count++
  const snapshot = current(draft) // keeps allocating instead of returning
})
```

The snapshot walker adds each copied value to the same Set it is traversing. Native Set iteration then visits the new value, copies it, and repeats. Frozen unchanged objects can instead leave both the draft and original in the snapshot.

Read from the existing shallow copy and write Set snapshots into a separate empty Set. This replaces draft values while preserving insertion order.

Six cases run with auto-freezing on and off, covering object and array values, nested Sets, membership changes, snapshot isolation, and reference sharing. Before the fix, 10 cases fail and two pass; afterward all 12 pass. A traversal guard keeps the regression tests from hanging. An uninstrumented production-build reproduction also fails before the fix and returns correctly afterward.

Validation on Node 25.2.1 / Yarn 1.22.22:
- `yarn test`: 3,848 source tests and 3,297 production-build tests passed, with eight existing skips in each suite; build and Flow passed.
- `yarn coverage`, `yarn test:perf`, Prettier for both changed files, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Source and test type checks passed with dependency declarations skipped and Node module resolution (ES2020 for the tests). Default `tsc --noEmit` still reports dependency-declaration errors identical to the unmodified baseline.

Prepared with AI assistance, including code, tests, and a separate AI review of the final diff.

test_patch:
diff --git a/__tests__/current.js b/__tests__/current.js
index 34143e8..600dd3c 100644
--- a/__tests__/current.js
+++ b/__tests__/current.js
@@ -1,4 +1,6 @@
+import {vi} from "vitest"
 import {
+	Immer,
 	setAutoFreeze,
 	current,
 	immerable,
@@ -244,3 +246,119 @@ function runTests(name) {
 		})
 	})
 }
+
+// Bound Set traversal so a regression cannot hang the test process.
+function takeSetSnapshot(draft) {
+	const forEach = Set.prototype.forEach
+	const guard = vi
+		.spyOn(Set.prototype, "forEach")
+		.mockImplementation(function (callback, thisArg) {
+			const size = this.size
+			let visited = 0
+			return forEach.call(this, (value, key, set) => {
+				if (++visited > size)
+					throw new Error("Set snapshot traversal grew beyond its initial size")
+				callback.call(thisArg, value, key, set)
+			})
+		})
+	try {
+		return current(draft)
+	} finally {
+		guard.mockRestore()
+	}
+}
+
+describe.each([true, false])(
+	"current Set snapshots - autoFreeze=%s",
+	autoFreeze => {
+		const {produce} = new Immer({autoFreeze})
+
+		it("snapshots modified objects in insertion order without leaking drafts", () => {
+			const changed = {count: 0}
+			const untouched = {count: 10}
+			const base = new Set([changed, "middle", untouched])
+			let snapshot
+			const next = produce(base, draft => {
+				const item = draft.values().next().value
+				item.count = 1
+				snapshot = takeSetSnapshot(draft)
+				const values = [...snapshot]
+				expect(values).toEqual([{count: 1}, "middle", untouched])
+				expect(values[2]).toBe(untouched)
+				expect(values.every(value => !isDraft(value))).toBe(true)
+				expect(Object.isFrozen(snapshot)).toBe(false)
+				expect(Object.isFrozen(values[0])).toBe(false)
+				item.count = 2
+				expect(values[0].count).toBe(1)
+			})
+			expect([...snapshot]).toEqual([{count: 1}, "middle", untouched])
+			expect([...next]).toEqual([{count: 2}, "middle", untouched])
+			expect(changed.count).toBe(0)
+		})
+
+		it("snapshots object Sets nested in a parent", () => {
+			const base = {items: new Set([{count: 0}])}
+			let snapshot
+			const next = produce(base, draft => {
+				const item = draft.items.values().next().value
+				item.count = 1
+				snapshot = takeSetSnapshot(draft)
+				item.count = 2
+			})
+			expect([...snapshot.items]).toEqual([{count: 1}])
+			expect([...next.items]).toEqual([{count: 2}])
+			expect([...base.items]).toEqual([{count: 0}])
+		})
+
+		it("keeps membership snapshots independent of later additions and deletions", () => {
+			const removed = {id: "removed"}
+			const kept = {id: "kept"}
+			const base = new Set([removed, kept])
+			let snapshot
+			const next = produce(base, draft => {
+				draft.delete(removed)
+				draft.add({id: "added"})
+				snapshot = takeSetSnapshot(draft)
+				expect([...snapshot]).toEqual([kept, {id: "added"}])
+				expect([...snapshot][0]).toBe(kept)
+				draft.clear()
+			})
+			expect([...snapshot]).toEqual([kept, {id: "added"}])
+			expect(next.size).toBe(0)
+			expect([...base]).toEqual([removed, kept])
+		})
+
+		it("snapshots arrays stored as Set values", () => {
+			const base = new Set([[1]])
+			let snapshot
+			produce(base, draft => {
+				const item = draft.values().next().value
+				item.push(2)
+				snapshot = takeSetSnapshot(draft)
+				item.push(3)
+			})
+			expect([...snapshot]).toEqual([[1, 2]])
+			expect([...base]).toEqual([[1]])
+		})
+
+		it("keeps unchanged frozen objects exactly once when adding a primitive", () => {
+			const item = freeze({count: 0})
+			const base = new Set([item])
+			let snapshot
+			produce(base, draft => {
+				draft.add(1)
+				snapshot = takeSetSnapshot(draft)
+			})
+			expect([...snapshot]).toEqual([item, 1])
+			expect([...snapshot][0]).toBe(item)
+		})
+
+		it("returns the original Set when its objects are only read", () => {
+			const base = new Set([{count: 0}])
+			produce(base, draft => {
+				expect(draft.values().next().value.count).toBe(0)
+				expect(takeSetSnapshot(draft)).toBe(base)
+			})
+		})
+	}
+)

pr.title: fix: snapshot array length before optimized filter callbacks
pr.body:
With array-method optimizations enabled, filtering an already modified draft visits elements appended by the predicate. Reading source.length on every iteration differs from Array.prototype.filter, which captures the initial length, and an appending predicate can keep extending the loop.

Capture the length before invoking the predicate. The regression compares plugin-enabled and regular behavior with auto-freezing enabled and disabled, including final draft and base contents.

Validation (Node.js 24.15.0, Windows): The two plugin-enabled regressions fail before the fix. Source suite: 4,015 passing, 8 skipped. npm run build passes. Built-bundle suite: 3,464 passing, 8 skipped.

AI assistance: this contribution was prepared with OpenAI Codex; the change and regression results were reviewed before submission.

problem_statement:
fix: snapshot array length before optimized filter callbacks

With array-method optimizations enabled, filtering an already modified draft visits elements appended by the predicate. Reading source.length on every iteration differs from Array.prototype.filter, which captures the initial length, and an appending predicate can keep extending the loop.

Capture the length before invoking the predicate. The regression compares plugin-enabled and regular behavior with auto-freezing enabled and disabled, including final draft and base contents.

Validation (Node.js 24.15.0, Windows): The two plugin-enabled regressions fail before the fix. Source suite: 4,015 passing, 8 skipped. npm run build passes. Built-bundle suite: 3,464 passing, 8 skipped.

AI assistance: this contribution was prepared with OpenAI Codex; the change and regression results were reviewed before submission.
test_patch:
diff --git a/__tests__/array-methods-filter-length.js b/__tests__/array-methods-filter-length.js
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..a52f376
--- /dev/null
+++ b/__tests__/array-methods-filter-length.js
@@ -0,0 +1,32 @@
+import {Immer, enableArrayMethods} from "../src/immer"
+import {clearPlugin, PluginArrayMethods} from "../src/internal"
+
+for (const enabled of [false, true]) {
+	for (const autoFreeze of [false, true]) {
+		describe(`filter length: plugin=${enabled}, autoFreeze=${autoFreeze}`, () => {
+			beforeEach(() => {
+				if (enabled) enableArrayMethods()
+				else clearPlugin(PluginArrayMethods)
+			})
+			afterEach(() => clearPlugin(PluginArrayMethods))
+
+			test("does not visit items appended by the predicate", () => {
+				const {produce} = new Immer({autoFreeze})
+				const base = [1, 2]
+				const visited = []
+				const result = produce(base, draft => {
+					draft.push(3)
+					const filtered = draft.filter((value, index) => {
+						visited.push(index)
+						if (index === 0) draft.push(4)
+						return true
+					})
+					expect(filtered).toEqual([1, 2, 3])
+				})
+				expect(visited).toEqual([0, 1, 2])
+				expect(result).toEqual([1, 2, 3, 4])
+				expect(base).toEqual([1, 2])
+			})
+		})
+	}
+}

pr.title: fix: skip patches of a draft discarded by writing its base value back

problem_statement:
fix: skip patches of a draft discarded by writing its base value back

Writing a base value back over a draft that was already modified discards the draft, and the produced state correctly keeps the original value. The patches, however, still contain the discarded draft's changes:

```js
enablePatches()

const child = {id: 1}
const base = {child}

const [next, patches] = produceWithPatches(base, draft => {
	draft.child.id = 2
	draft.child = child // put the base value back
})

next // {child: {id: 1}}
patches // [{op: "replace", path: ["child", "id"], value: 2}]
applyPatches(base, patches) // {child: {id: 2}}
```

The same happens for array elements, Map entries, and drafts nested inside the discarded one. Anything that replays the patches (an undo stack, a server applying client patches, a second copy of the state) ends up with a value the producer never kept. This is a regression from the finalization rewrite in #1183; before it, the patches above were empty.

`getPath` checks whether the value at a draft's key still belongs to that draft, and accepted the draft, its copy, or its base. A draft is stored in its parent's copy as soon as it is created, so the base can only be back at that key when the original value was written back, which is exactly when the draft has been discarded. Accepting only the draft or its copy skips patch generation for discarded drafts, including the drafts nested inside them.

The regression tests cover objects, nested drafts, arrays and Maps. Before the fix, 8 of the 16 cases fail; afterwards all of them pass.

Validation (Node 26.5.0, Yarn 1.22.22, Windows):
- `yarn test`: 4,212 source tests and 3,661 production-build tests passed, with 8 existing skips in each suite; build and Flow passed.
- `yarn test:perf`, Prettier for both changed files, and `git diff --check` passed.
- A randomized round-trip check (random mutations on nested objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, verifying that the patches reproduce the result and the inverse patches restore the base) failed on this pattern before the fix and passes 60,000 runs afterwards.
test_patch:
diff --git a/__tests__/patch.js b/__tests__/patch.js
index d6afcbe..c4aff9a 100644
--- a/__tests__/patch.js
+++ b/__tests__/patch.js
@@ -1637,3 +1637,60 @@ describe("assigning a base value back over its own draft", () => {
 		{a: {child: {id: 1}, other: 1}}
 	)
 })
+
+describe("assigning a base value back over a modified draft", () => {
+	// Writing the base value back discards the draft, including its changes,
+	// so those changes must not show up in the patches either.
+	const objectChild = {id: 1}
+	runPatchTests(
+		"object",
+		{child: objectChild, other: 0},
+		d => {
+			d.child.id = 2
+			d.child = objectChild
+			d.other = 1
+		},
+		[{op: "replace", path: ["other"], value: 1}],
+		[{op: "replace", path: ["other"], value: 0}],
+		{child: {id: 1}, other: 1}

pr.title: fix: honor class-only shallow copy in Immer constructor
pr.body:
## Summary

The constructor accepts useStrictShallowCopy: "class_only" in its public type but silently drops the setting. Apply it just like the equivalent setter. The regression verifies that class copies keep their non-enumerable properties and plain object copies still omit them.

## Validation

The new regression fails on main and passes with the fix. Source suite: 4,213 passed, 8 skipped. JS bundles build. Declaration generation fails with the installed TypeScript version on both main and this branch due to existing Map/Set iterator errors in mapset.ts.

## AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with the implementation and regression test. The baseline failure, passing tests, and final diff were checked locally.

problem_statement:
fix: honor class-only shallow copy in Immer constructor

## Summary

The constructor accepts useStrictShallowCopy: "class_only" in its public type but silently drops the setting. Apply it just like the equivalent setter. The regression verifies that class copies keep their non-enumerable properties and plain object copies still omit them.

## Validation

The new regression fails on main and passes with the fix. Source suite: 4,213 passed, 8 skipped. JS bundles build. Declaration generation fails with the installed TypeScript version on both main and this branch due to existing Map/Set iterator errors in mapset.ts.

## AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with the implementation and regression test. The baseline failure, passing tests, and final diff were checked locally.
test_patch:
diff --git a/__tests__/not-strict-copy.ts b/__tests__/not-strict-copy.ts
index 9414302..4f040d9 100644
--- a/__tests__/not-strict-copy.ts
+++ b/__tests__/not-strict-copy.ts
@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@
 import {
+	Immer,
 	immerable,
 	produce,
 	setUseStrictShallowCopy,
@@ -73,3 +74,29 @@ describe.each([true, false, "class_only" as const])(
 		})
 	}
 )
+
+test("honors the constructor class_only shallow copy mode", () => {
+	const immer = new Immer({useStrictShallowCopy: "class_only"})
+
+	class Example {
+		[immerable] = true
+		count = 0
+	}
+
+	const instance = new Example()
+	const plain = {count: 0}
+	Object.defineProperty(instance, "hidden", {value: 42})
+	Object.defineProperty(plain, "hidden", {value: 42})
+
+	const nextInstance = immer.produce(instance, draft => {
+		draft.count++
+	})
+	const nextPlain = immer.produce(plain, draft => {
+		draft.count++
+	})
+
+	expect(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(nextInstance, "hidden")?.value).toBe(
+		42
+	)
+	expect(Object.hasOwn(nextPlain, "hidden")).toBe(false)
+})

pr.title: Avoid duplicate trailing delimiter matches
pr.body:
Fixes #441.

`pathToRegexp('/about/')` currently appends the optional trailing delimiter after a source that already ends in `/`, so the generated matcher accepts `/about//`. This moves the optional trailing delimiter into each flattened alternative and skips it when that alternative already ends with the configured delimiter.

Verification:
- `./node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/index.spec.ts -t '/test//'`
- `./node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/index.spec.ts`
- `npm run build`
- `npm run size`
- `git diff --check`

Note: I also attempted `npm test`; it reached 477 passing Vitest tests but the local ReDoS helper binary requires GLIBC_2.32/GLIBC_2.34 while this host has glibc 2.28, so that command exits with `recheck-linux-x64` EPIPE errors in this environment.

issue_texts.441:
regexp should not end with both explicit end-slash and optional end-slash

Hello and thanks for this package. When the original path ends with an end-slash (ex '/about/') the returned regexp ends with both a required and an optional end-slash; I believe, instead, it should end with only one end-slash; optional or required.

Instead of this,
```javascript
pathToRegexp('/about/').regexp // /^(?:\/about\/)(?:\/$)?$/i
```

One of these would be better,
```javascript
pathToRegexp('/about/').regexp // /^(?:\/about)(?:\/$)?$/i
pathToRegexp('/about/').regexp // /^(?:\/about\/)$/i
```

pr.title: fix: reject wildcard array that compiles to an empty path
pr.body:
`compile` for a wildcard accepts an array whose only content is empty, and silently returns a path the same pattern can never match:

```js
compile("/*foo")({ foo: [""] }); //=> "/"
match("/*foo")("/");             //=> false
```

The value is lost with no error. This is the array counterpart of the empty-string param case rejected in #444.

A wildcard's value domain is exactly what `match` produces — `capturedValue.split(delimiter)` — and `match` can never yield `[""]`, since the capture group requires at least one character. So there is no input for which `[""]` is a correct value; `compile` should reject it rather than emit an unmatchable path.

The fix throws when the joined output is empty. Arrays that contain empty segments but still produce content (e.g. `["a", ""]` → `"/a/"`, `["route", "nested", ""]` → `"/route/nested/"`) are what `match` returns for trailing/empty segments and continue to round-trip unchanged.

Adds a regression test.

pr.title: Fix stringify lookahead across empty text tokens
pr.body:
`stringify()` can merge literal text into a parameter name when an empty text token sits between them. For custom `TokenData` containing `param("foo"), text(""), text("bar")`, it emits `:foobar` instead of `:"foo"bar`. Compiling the serialized path then rejects the original `foo` parameter.

Skip empty text tokens when looking ahead to decide whether a name needs quotes. Adds parameter and wildcard regressions with ASCII and astral identifier suffixes, plus delimiter and end-of-input controls. Each case also checks that compilation survives the stringify round trip.

Validation: `npm test` on Node 18, 20, 24, and 26; 492 tests pass with build, type checking, formatting, coverage, and the 2 kB size limit.

pr.title: fix(diff,counting): stop inherited Object.prototype keys from corrupting results
pr.body:
`diff` and `counting` both used a plain object literal (`{}`) as a lookup/accumulator, so any identity that collides with an inherited `Object.prototype` key is read as if it were already present.

`group` was fixed for exactly this in #427 (`Object.create(null)`); these two were missed.

### `diff` — items are silently dropped

```ts
diff(['toString', 'constructor', 'a'], ['b'])
// actual:   ['a']
// expected: ['toString', 'constructor', 'a']
```

`bKeys[identity(a)]` resolves to `Object.prototype.toString` (a function, truthy), so the filter removes the item even though `other` never contained it. Same for `constructor`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, `__proto__`, etc. This bites any real use where the identity is a user-supplied string — field names, slugs, i18n keys, route names.

Fixed by using a `Set`, which has no prototype keys.

### `counting` — the tally starts from an inherited value

```ts
counting(['toString', 'toString', 'a'], x => x)
// actual:   { toString: 'function toString() { [native code] }11', a: 1 }
// expected: { toString: 2, a: 1 }
```

`acc[id] ?? 0` finds the inherited method instead of `undefined`, so the first `+ 1` string-concatenates and every subsequent count builds on that garbage. Fixed with `Object.create(null)`, matching `group`.

The `reduce` calls became plain `for...of` loops in the process, which is a touch faster and easier to read; behaviour is otherwise unchanged.

### Validation

- Added one regression test per function. Both fail on `master` and pass with the fix.
- `pnpm test` → 182 files, 909 tests passing, type checks clean, coverage still 100%.
- `biome check` clean on the four touched files.

No public API or type signature changes.

gold_patch:
diff --git a/src/array/counting.ts b/src/array/counting.ts
index 4020930..daca086 100644
--- a/src/array/counting.ts
+++ b/src/array/counting.ts
@@ -14,15 +14,13 @@ export function counting<T, TId extends string | number | symbol>(
   array: readonly T[],
   identity: (item: T) => TId,
 ): Record<TId, number> {
+  const counts = Object.create(null) as Record<TId, number>
   if (!array) {
-    return {} as Record<TId, number>
+    return counts
   }
-  return array.reduce(
-    (acc, item) => {
-      const id = identity(item)
-      acc[id] = (acc[id] ?? 0) + 1
-      return acc
-    },
-    {} as Record<TId, number>,
-  )
+  for (const item of array) {
+    const id = identity(item)
+    counts[id] = (counts[id] ?? 0) + 1
+  }
+  return counts
 }

pr.title: fix(selectFirst): map a matched undefined element
pr.body:
## Summary

`selectFirst` used `array.find(...)` and then checked `found === undefined` to decide whether anything matched. `find` returns `undefined` both when nothing matches and when the matched element is itself `undefined`, so in the second case the mapper was never called:

```ts
const mapper = (x: number | undefined) => (x === undefined ? 'none' : x)
selectFirst([undefined, 1], mapper, () => true) // was undefined, now 'none'
selectFirst([undefined, 1], mapper)             // was undefined, now 'none'
```

The fix uses `findIndex` and checks `foundIndex === -1`, so the decision is based on whether an index matched, not on the element's value. Signature, types, and all other behavior are unchanged. A regression test covers both the explicit-condition and default-condition cases.

This change was made with the help of Claude Code; I reviewed and tested it.

## Related issue, if any:

Fixes #483

## For any code change,

- [ ] Related documentation has been updated, if needed
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Release notes in [next-minor.md](.github/next-minor.md) or [next-major.md](.github/next-major.md) have been added, if needed

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

issue_texts.483:
selectFirst skips the mapper when the matched element is undefined

`selectFirst` already tracks `foundIndex`, then still keys off the found *value*:

```ts
const found = array.find((item, index) => {
  foundIndex = index
  return condition ? condition(item, index) : mapper(item, index) != null
})
return found === undefined ? undefined : mapper(found, foundIndex)
```

`Array.prototype.find` returns `undefined` both when nothing matched and when the matching element *is* `undefined`. In the second case the mapper never runs.

Without a condition, the docs say it selects the first mapped value that is non-nullish. A mapper that produces a non-nullish result from an `undefined` element is still skipped.

### Repro (current main / 12.9.4)

```ts
import { selectFirst } from 'radashi'

selectFirst(
  [undefined, 1],
  x => (x === undefined ? 'none' : x),
  () => true,
)
// actual:   undefined
// expected: 'none'

selectFirst(
  [undefined, 1],
  x => (x === undefined ? 'none' : x),
)
// same result — mapper is never applied to the matched undefined element
```

### Suggested fix

Treat `foundIndex !== -1` as the hit, not `found !== undefined`. Initialize `foundIndex` to `-1` (already the case) and only skip the mapper when nothing matched.

Happy to send a PR if that's useful.

diff --git a/tests/array/selectFirst.test.ts b/tests/array/selectFirst.test.ts

+      (_x, idx) => idx === 1,

pr.title: fix(toggle): remove a matching undefined element instead of appending
pr.body:
Fixes #482

`toggle` decides add vs. remove with `array.find(matcher)` and tests the result against `undefined`. `Array.prototype.find` returns `undefined` both when nothing matched and when the matching element *is* `undefined`, so a `toKey` matcher that hits an `undefined` slot first takes the append branch even though a match exists.

```ts
toggle([undefined, 'a'], 'b', () => 'k')
// before: [undefined, 'a', 'b']
// after:  []   // every element shares the key, so all matches are removed
```

`item === undefined` is already special-cased earlier in the function, so this is only reachable through a `toKey` callback.

### Change

`find` → `findIndex`, compared against `-1`. The removal branch still uses the same `matcher` with `filter`, so multi-match removal behaviour is unchanged. No API or type changes.

### Validation

- `npx vitest run tests/array/` → 45 files, 206 tests passing, no type errors.
- The added test fails on `main` (`expected [ undefined, 'a', 'b' ] to deeply equal []`) and passes with the fix.
- `node scripts/run lint` → Biome clean. The only findings are pre-existing cspell warnings in `tests/string/deburr.test.ts`, untouched here.


## Bundle impact

| Status | File | Size [^1337] | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | `src/array/toggle.ts` | 255 | +1 (+0%) |

[^1337]: Function size includes the `import` dependencies of the function.

pr.title: fix(memo): stop inherited Object.prototype keys from being treated as cache hits
pr.body:
## Summary

`memo` stores its cache in a plain object literal (`{}`) and checks `cache[key] !== undefined` to decide whether it has a cached entry. When a custom `key` function returns a string that matches an inherited `Object.prototype` property, the lookup finds that inherited property. `memo` then treats it as a cached entry, never calls the wrapped function, and returns `undefined`:

```ts
const fn = memo((key: string) => `value:${key}`, { key: key => key })
fn('constructor')    // was undefined, now 'value:constructor'
fn('toString')       // was undefined, now 'value:toString'
fn('hasOwnProperty') // was undefined, now 'value:hasOwnProperty'
fn('__proto__')      // was undefined, now 'value:__proto__'
```

Reproduced on 12.9.5. In each of these cases the wrapped function is never called. For `__proto__`, the write after a miss would also replace the cache object's prototype instead of storing an entry. The default key (`JSON.stringify({ args })`) always starts with `{"args"`, so this only affects custom `key` functions. Those often return user-supplied strings such as ids, slugs, or field names.

The fix creates the cache with `Object.create(null)`, the same approach used for `group` (#427) and `counting` (#481). With no prototype there are no inherited keys, so the existing `!== undefined` check becomes an own-key check. I didn't switch to `Object.hasOwn` because the `es2017` lib target doesn't include it, and nothing more is needed here.

A cached `undefined` result was already treated as a hit, and it still is. The cache stores `{ exp, value }` entry objects, so the check never looks at the stored value itself. I added a test that locks this in alongside the regression test. The new prototype-key test fails on `main` and passes with the fix.

- `pnpm test`: 182 files, 918 tests passing, type checks clean, coverage still 100%.
- `biome check` and `cspell` are clean on the touched files.

No public API or type signature changes.

This change was made with the help of Claude Code; I reviewed and tested it.

## Related issue, if any:

None filed. This follows #481.

## For any code change,

- [ ] Related documentation has been updated, if needed
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Release notes in [next-minor.md](.github/next-minor.md) or [next-major.md](.github/next-major.md) have been added, if needed

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

gold_patch:
diff --git a/src/curry/memo.ts b/src/curry/memo.ts
index d44c806..4e3099d 100644
--- a/src/curry/memo.ts
+++ b/src/curry/memo.ts
@@ -61,5 +61,10 @@ export function memo<TArgs extends any[], TResult>(
   func: (...args: TArgs) => TResult,
   options: MemoOptions<NoInfer<TArgs>> = {},
 ): (...args: TArgs) => TResult {
-  return memoize({}, func, options.key ?? null, options.ttl ?? null)
+  return memoize(
+    Object.create(null),
+    func,
+    options.key ?? null,
+    options.ttl ?? null,
+  )
 }

+    const fn = vi.fn(() => undefined)
+    const func = _.memo(fn)
+    func()

+  })

pr.title: fix!: align AggregateError polyfill with native behavior
pr.body:
## Summary

When native `AggregateError` is unavailable, the fallback currently ignores the supplied message, rejects non-array iterables, borrows an inner error's stack, and throws when the input contains `null` or `undefined`. It also cannot be called without `new`, despite the exported call signature.

Align the fallback with native behavior: copy iterable inputs into a non-enumerable `errors` property, preserve the supplied message and an independent stack, support `options.cause`, and support both ordinary calls and subclasses. Set the constructor and prototype properties to match the native error. The native constructor is still used whenever it exists.

Run the same behavioral tests against the fallback and native constructor, including property descriptors, arbitrary error values, invalid inputs, and evaluation order. Before the fix, 21 of the 62 focused checks failed. After the fix:

- `pnpm test`: 976 tests passed across 182 files; 100% statements, branches, functions, and lines.
- Source, test, and benchmark TypeScript checks and full Biome checks passed; spelling checks on the changed source and test files passed.
- Full `pnpm lint --base f5aa29a` hits 256 pre-existing spelling diagnostics, reproduced identically on the unmodified base. The lint runner then cancels its remaining JSR preflight. This is separate from the passing tests and build.
- Build and ESM/CommonJS fallback smoke checks passed.

## Related issue, if any:

Fixes #379.

## For any code change,

- [x] Related documentation has been updated, if needed
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [x] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed (not needed for this compatibility fix)
- [x] Release notes in [next-minor.md](.github/next-minor.md) or [next-major.md](.github/next-major.md) have been added, if needed

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

Yes, in environments using the fallback. Its name becomes `AggregateError`, its default message becomes empty, and its stack identifies the aggregate's creation rather than the first inner error. `errors` becomes a non-enumerable copy instead of an alias of the input array. Non-iterable inputs (including an omitted argument) now throw `TypeError`, matching native behavior.

Pass `[]` when there are no errors, pass an explicit message when needed, and inspect `error.errors` for individual errors and their stacks. Environments already using the native constructor retain their behavior.


## Bundle impact

| Status | File | Size [^1337] | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | `src/oop/AggregateError.ts` | 697 | +400 (+135%) |

[^1337]: Function size includes the `import` dependencies of the function.

'' this.name = `AggregateError(${name}...)` this.message = `AggregateError with ${errors.length} errors` this.stack = errors.find(e => e.stack)?.stack ?? this.stack! this.errors = errors } } ```

@@ -1,10 +1,19 @@
 interface AggregateError extends Error {
   errors: any[]
+  cause?: unknown
 }
 
 interface AggregateErrorConstructor {
-  new (errors: Iterable<any>, message?: string): AggregateError
-  (errors: Iterable<any>, message?: string): AggregateError
+  new (
+    errors: Iterable<any>,
+    message?: string,
+    options?: { cause?: unknown },
+  ): AggregateError
+  (
+    errors: Iterable<any>,
+    message?: string,
+    options?: { cause?: unknown },
+  ): AggregateError
   readonly prototype: AggregateError
 }
 
@@ -19,24 +28,56 @@ declare const globalThis: {
  * As this error type is relatively new, it's not available in every
  * environment supported by Radashi (last checked on July 20, 2024).
  * When it's not globally defined, Radashi provides a polyfill.
+ * The polyfill copies the iterable of errors and supports an optional
+ * message and `options.cause`, like the native constructor.
  *
  * @see https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/AggregateError
  * @version 12.2.0
  */
 const AggregateErrorOrPolyfill: AggregateErrorConstructor =
-  /* @__PURE__ */ (() =>
-    globalThis.AggregateError ??
-    (class AggregateError extends Error {
-      errors: Error[]
-      constructor(errors: Error[] = []) {
-        super()
-        const name = errors.find(e => e.name)?.name ?? ''
-        this.name = `AggregateError(${name}...)`
-        this.message = `AggregateError with ${errors.length} errors`
-        this.stack = errors.find(e => e.stack)?.stack ?? this.stack!
-        this.errors = errors
+  /* @__PURE__ */ (() => {
+    if (globalThis.AggregateError) {
+      return globalThis.AggregateError
+    }
+
+    function AggregateError(
+      errors: Iterable<any>,
+      message?: string,
+      options: { cause?: unknown } | undefined = undefined,
+    ): AggregateError {
+      const error = Reflect.construct(
+        Error,
+        [message],
+        new.target ?? AggregateError,
+      )
+      if (
+        options !== null &&
+        (typeof options === 'object' || typeof options === 'function') &&
+        'cause' in options
+      ) {
+        Object.defineProperty(error, 'cause', {
+          value: options.cause,
+          writable: true,
+          configurable: true,
+        })
       }
-    } as unknown as AggregateErrorConstructor))()
+      Object.defineProperty(error, 'errors', {
+        value: [...errors],
+        writable: true,
+        configurable: true,
+      })
+      return error
+    }
+
+    Object.setPrototypeOf(AggregateError, Error)
+    Object.setPrototypeOf(AggregateError.prototype, Error.prototype)
+    Object.defineProperty(AggregateError, 'prototype', { writable: false })
+    Object.defineProperties(AggregateError.prototype, {
+      name: { value: 'AggregateError', writable: true, configurable: true },
+      message: { value: '', writable: true, configurable: true },
+    })
+    return AggregateError as unknown as AggregateErrorConstructor
+  })()

pr.title: fix(parallel): stop treating falsy rejections as success
pr.body:
## Summary

`parallel(1, [1], async () => { throw 0 })` resolves with `[undefined]` instead of rejecting. Collect success and failure records separately so falsy rejection reasons are not mistaken for successful results.

The five regression cases failed before the change. All 927 tests and type tests pass with 100% coverage; full source/test Biome lint, changed-file formatting, TypeScript and CJS/ESM/declaration builds pass. The full run used two workers and a 30-second timeout after the default timeout expired in two AggregateError tests. The Windows lint wrapper cannot find its command directory, so Biome was run directly.

Native AggregateError preserves `0`, `false`, `''`, `null`, and `undefined`. The existing fallback preserves the first three; its separate null/undefined limitation remains covered by #487. The browser matrix was not run.

## Related issue, if any:

None.

## For any code change,

- [ ] Related documentation has been updated, if needed
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Release notes in [next-minor.md](.github/next-minor.md) or [next-major.md](.github/next-major.md) have been added, if needed

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

pr.title: fix(round): preserve infinity with nonzero precision
pr.body:
## Summary

I noticed that `round(Infinity, 1)` returned `NaN`, even though `round(Infinity)` kept `Infinity`. Negative infinity had the same problem.

I kept non-finite values out of the exponent-shifting step and let the existing rounding callback handle them. I added regression tests for positive and negative precision; they failed before the fix.

I ran `pnpm test` (full coverage), `pnpm build`, `pnpm format` and `pnpm lint`; lint's spelling check reported the same errors on untouched `main`.

![Rounding output before and after the fix](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Don-Yin/radashi/546f3f9438fa22968fbae38d455112c3c0446756/round-output.png)

## Related issue, if any:

None.

## For any code change,

- [ ] Related documentation has been updated, if needed
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed
- [ ] Release notes in [next-minor.md](.github/next-minor.md) or [next-major.md](.github/next-major.md) have been added, if needed

No documentation, benchmark or release-note changes were needed for this bug fix.

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

+    'preserves non-finite values with precision %i',
+    precision => {
+      for (const strategy of [Math.round, Math.ceil, Math.floor]) {
+        expect(_.round(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY, precision, strategy)).toBe(
+          Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY,
+        )
+        expect(_.round(Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, precision, strategy)).toBe(
+          Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY,
+        )
+        expect(_.round(Number.NaN, precision, strategy)).toBeNaN()
+      }
+    },
+  )
+

     expect(_.round(1e50)).toBe(1e50)

pr.title: fix(promiseMemo): retain replacement cache entries after stale rejection
pr.body:
## Summary

When an in-flight promise expires, a later call stores a replacement for the same key. If the old promise subsequently rejects, its rejection handler deletes that replacement, causing an unnecessary third invocation.

Only evict the cache entry if it is still the entry owned by the rejecting promise. The regression uses controlled promises and fake time to exercise this ordering through `promiseMemo`.

## Related issue, if any:

No existing issue found for this race.

## For any code change,

- [x] Related documentation has been updated, if needed (no API change)
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [x] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed (not needed for this rejection-path guard)
- [x] Release notes in next-minor.md or next-major.md have been added, if needed (patch bug fix)

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

Validation: the regression calls the source three times before the fix, instead of two. All 184 test files / 949 tests pass afterward with 100% statement, branch, function and line coverage. Build, source/test type checking and targeted Biome checks pass. Targeted spelling check reports the pre-existing `Simuate` typo in the function's example.

AI assistance: this change and its regression tests were developed with OpenAI Codex. The listed checks were run locally.


## Bundle impact

| Status | File | Size [^1337] | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | `src/async/promiseMemo.ts` | 324 | +12 (+4%) |

[^1337]: Function size includes the `import` dependencies of the function.

test_patch:
diff --git a/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts b/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts
index d33cefe..fe372d0 100644
--- a/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts
+++ b/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts
@@ -89,3 +89,28 @@ describe('promiseMemo', () => {
     expect(func).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2)
   })
 })
+
+test('an expired rejection does not evict the replacement promise', async () => {
+  vi.useFakeTimers()
+  try {
+    const first = _.withResolvers<string>()
+    const second = Promise.resolve('fresh')
+    const source = vi
+      .fn()
+      .mockReturnValueOnce(first.promise)
+      .mockReturnValue(second)
+    const memoized = _.promiseMemo(source, { ttl: 100 })
+
+    const stale = memoized()
+    vi.advanceTimersByTime(101)
+    expect(memoized()).toBe(second)
+
+    first.reject(new Error('expired request failed'))
+    await expect(stale).rejects.toThrow('expired request failed')
+
+    expect(memoized()).toBe(second)
+    expect(source).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2)
+  } finally {
+    vi.useRealTimers()
+  }
+})

pr.title: fix(promiseMemo): support prototype-named custom cache keys
pr.body:
## Summary

With a custom key such as `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, or `__proto__`, `promiseMemo` treats an inherited Object.prototype property as an existing cache entry and returns undefined without calling the function.

Use a null-prototype object for the default cache, consistent with the synchronous `memo` fix in #486. Tests verify the returned promise, resolved value and reuse for all four keys.

## Related issue, if any:

Related to #486, which fixes synchronous `memo`; this PR covers `promiseMemo`.

## For any code change,

- [x] Related documentation has been updated, if needed (no API change)
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [x] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed (no algorithm change)
- [x] Release notes in next-minor.md or next-major.md have been added, if needed (patch bug fix)

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

Validation: all four new cases fail on the original implementation. Afterward, all 184 test files / 952 tests pass with 100% statement, branch, function and line coverage. Build, source/test type checking and targeted Biome checks pass.

AI assistance: this change and its regression tests were developed with OpenAI Codex. The listed checks were run locally.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | `src/async/promiseMemo.ts` | 341 | +17 (+5%) |

test_patch:
diff --git a/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts b/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts
index fe372d0..3cee82b 100644
--- a/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts
+++ b/tests/async/promiseMemo.test.ts
@@ -114,3 +114,15 @@ test('an expired rejection does not evict the replacement promise', async () =>
     vi.useRealTimers()
   }
 })
+
+test.each(['constructor', 'toString', 'hasOwnProperty', '__proto__'])(
+  'memoizes promises whose custom key is %s',
+  async key => {
+    const source = vi.fn(async (value: string) => value)
+    const memoized = _.promiseMemo(source, { key: value => value })
+    const first = memoized(key)
+    await expect(first).resolves.toBe(key)
+    expect(memoized(key)).toBe(first)
+    expect(source).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
+  },
+)

pr.title: fix(Semaphore): drain queued requests while capacity remains
pr.body:
## Summary

Releasing a weighted Semaphore permit currently wakes only one queued request, even when enough capacity remains for other waiting requests. For example, releasing weight 4 with queued weights 1, 2, 1 wakes only the first request and leaves capacity idle. Drain the queue in order until the next request cannot fit. The change keeps the capacity reservation synchronous.

Validation: The new regression fails on main (only weight 1 is acquired instead of 1, 2, 1). Tests also cover stopping at a request that cannot fit and restoring total capacity. Full suite: 184 files / 950 tests, 100% coverage; type tests, tsc --noEmit, targeted Biome checks and build pass.

## Related issue, if any:

No existing issue was found for this specific behavior; related issues and existing PRs were checked before implementation.

test_patch:
diff --git a/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts b/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts
index 70d064a..deaae84 100644
--- a/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts
+++ b/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts
@@ -169,3 +169,40 @@ describe('Semaphore', () => {
     await expect(() => semaphore.acquire()).rejects.toThrow(rejectionError)
   })
 })
+
+test('releases all queued requests that fit the returned capacity', async () => {
+  const semaphore = new Semaphore(4)
+  const held = await semaphore.acquire({ weight: 4 })
+  const acquired: SemaphorePermit[] = []
+  const requests = [1, 2, 1].map(weight =>
+    semaphore.acquire({ weight }).then(permit => acquired.push(permit)),
+  )
+  held.release()
+  await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
+  expect(acquired.map(permit => permit.weight)).toEqual([1, 2, 1])
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(0)
+  expect(semaphore.queueLength).toBe(0)
+  await Promise.all(requests)
+  acquired.forEach(permit => permit.release())
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(4)
+})
+
+test('stops draining when the next queued request does not fit', async () => {
+  const semaphore = new Semaphore(4)
+  const first = await semaphore.acquire({ weight: 3 })
+  const second = await semaphore.acquire()
+  const acquired: SemaphorePermit[] = []
+  const requests = [1, 3].map(weight =>
+    semaphore.acquire({ weight }).then(permit => acquired.push(permit)),
+  )
+  first.release()
+  await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
+  expect(acquired.map(permit => permit.weight)).toEqual([1])
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(2)
+  expect(semaphore.queueLength).toBe(1)
+  second.release()
+  await Promise.all(requests)
+  expect(acquired.map(permit => permit.weight)).toEqual([1, 3])
+  acquired.forEach(permit => permit.release())
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(4)
+})

pr.title: fix(Semaphore): honor already aborted acquisition signals
pr.body:
## Summary

Semaphore.acquire accepts an already-aborted signal, taking capacity or leaving a request queued indefinitely. It also attaches a listener for immediately acquired permits to a promise that is never settled. Check the existing aborted state before acquiring, and attach abort listeners only when the request must wait. The optional aborted property preserves compatibility with existing custom signal implementations.

Validation: Three new regression cases fail on main. Coverage includes pre-aborted acquisition with available/exhausted capacity, listener lifetime and successful queued acquisition. Full suite: 184 files / 952 tests, 100% coverage; type tests, tsc --noEmit, targeted Biome checks and build pass.

## Related issue, if any:

No existing issue was found for this specific behavior; related issues and existing PRs were checked before implementation.

diff --git a/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts b/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts
index deaae84..f5ff337 100644
--- a/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts
+++ b/tests/oop/Semaphore.test.ts
@@ -206,3 +206,62 @@ test('stops draining when the next queued request does not fit', async () => {
   acquired.forEach(permit => permit.release())
   expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(4)
 })
+
+test('rejects an already aborted signal without consuming capacity', async () => {
+  const semaphore = new Semaphore(2)
+  const controller = new AbortController()
+  const reason = new Error('cancelled')
+  controller.abort(reason)
+  await expect(semaphore.acquire({ signal: controller.signal })).rejects.toBe(
+    reason,
+  )
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(2)
+  expect(semaphore.queueLength).toBe(0)
+})
+
+test('does not queue an already aborted acquisition when capacity is exhausted', async () => {
+  const semaphore = new Semaphore(1)
+  const held = await semaphore.acquire()
+  const controller = new AbortController()
+  controller.abort('cancelled')
+  const rejected = vi.fn()
+  const fulfilled = vi.fn()
+  const pending = semaphore
+    .acquire({ signal: controller.signal })
+    .then(fulfilled, rejected)
+  try {
+    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
+    expect(rejected).toHaveBeenCalledWith('cancelled')
+    expect(fulfilled).not.toHaveBeenCalled()
+    expect(semaphore.queueLength).toBe(0)
+  } finally {
+    held.release()
+    await pending
+  }
+})
+
+test('does not retain an abort listener for an immediately acquired permit', async () => {
+  const semaphore = new Semaphore(1)
+  const controller = new AbortController()
+  const add = vi.spyOn(controller.signal, 'addEventListener')
+  const permit = await semaphore.acquire({ signal: controller.signal })
+  expect(add).not.toHaveBeenCalled()
+  controller.abort()
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(0)
+  permit.release()
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(1)
+})
+
+test('removes the abort listener after a queued acquisition succeeds', async () => {
+  const semaphore = new Semaphore(1)
+  const held = await semaphore.acquire()
+  const controller = new AbortController()
+  const remove = vi.spyOn(controller.signal, 'removeEventListener')
+  const pending = semaphore.acquire({ signal: controller.signal })
+  held.release()
+  const permit = await pending
+  expect(remove).toHaveBeenCalledOnce()
+  controller.abort()
+  expect(semaphore.capacity).toBe(0)
+  permit.release()
+})

pr.title: fix(retry): check cancellation before starting attempts
pr.body:
## Summary

A pre-aborted signal still invokes the operation, and aborting during the retry delay starts another operation before rejecting. Check the signal at the start of every attempt, preserving the existing post-operation check.

## Validation

Both new cancellation regressions fail before the fix. Full suite: 184 files, 961 tests, 100% coverage. TypeScript, build and targeted Biome formatting pass.

## Related issue, if any:

None found; reproduced from the public retry API.

## For any code change,

- [x] Related documentation has been updated, if needed (existing API behavior is restored)
- [x] Related tests have been added or updated, if needed
- [x] Related benchmarks have been added or updated, if needed (not needed for this control-flow fix)
- [x] Release notes have been added, if needed (bug fix; no minor/major release note)

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

No

This patch and its regression tests were developed with OpenAI Codex assistance. The failing baseline, passing tests, and final diff were checked locally.

test_patch:
diff --git a/tests/async/retry.test.ts b/tests/async/retry.test.ts
index 7d3194d..84204e7 100644
--- a/tests/async/retry.test.ts
+++ b/tests/async/retry.test.ts
@@ -135,4 +135,32 @@ describe('retry', () => {
 
     expect.fail('error should have been thrown')
   })
+  test('does not start an attempt with an already aborted signal', async () => {
+    const controller = new AbortController()
+    const reason = new Error('cancelled')
+    controller.abort(reason)
+    const operation = vi.fn(async () => 'unexpected')
+    await expect(
+      _.retry({ signal: controller.signal }, operation),
+    ).rejects.toBe(reason)
+    expect(operation).not.toHaveBeenCalled()
+  })
+
+  test('does not start another attempt after cancellation during the delay', async () => {
+    const controller = new AbortController()
+    const reason = new Error('cancelled during delay')
+    const operation = vi.fn(async () => {
+      throw new Error('retry me')
+    })
+    const pending = _.retry(
+      { signal: controller.signal, delay: 100, times: 3 },
+      operation,
+    )
+    const rejected = expect(pending).rejects.toBe(reason)
+    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(0)
+    controller.abort(reason)
+    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100)
+    await rejected
+    expect(operation).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
+  })
 })

pr.title: fix(retry): stop on falsy exit reasons
pr.body:
## Summary

Calling exit(undefined), exit(null), exit(false), exit(0), or exit("") retries the operation and ultimately rejects with the internal wrapper. Detect the exit marker by property presence so all exit reasons stop immediately and are preserved.

## Validation

All five new regressions fail before the fix. Full suite: 184 files, 964 tests, 100% coverage. TypeScript, build and targeted Biome formatting pass.

## Related issue, if any:

None found; reproduced from the public retry API.

No

pr.title: fix: populate `error.path` for values inside promises in `stringifyAsync`
pr.body:
The README says you can find the offending value by reading `error.path`, and for `stringify` you can. Anything reached through a promise comes back empty though. `{ foo: { array: [() => {}] } }` gives `.foo.array[0]`, and the same function sat behind a `Promise.resolve` gives `''` out of `stringifyAsync`. Nested deeper it's worse than empty: `{ foo: Promise.resolve({ bar: Promise.resolve({ invalid() {} }) }) }` reports `.invalid`, which looks like a real path and isnt one.

`keys` is pushed and popped as the synchronous walk goes, and a promises contents get flattened in a callback that only runs once that walk has finished unwinding it. So this captures the path at the thenable and puts it back for the length of the callback.

Without the `try/finally` a sibling promise that throws first leaves its keys on the array, and `{ a: <slow promise of a function>, b: Promise.resolve(() => {}) }` reports `.b.a` insted of `.a`.

problem_statement:
fix: populate `error.path` for values inside promises in `stringifyAsync`

The README says you can find the offending value by reading `error.path`, and for `stringify` you can. Anything reached through a promise comes back empty though. `{ foo: { array: [() => {}] } }` gives `.foo.array[0]`, and the same function sat behind a `Promise.resolve` gives `''` out of `stringifyAsync`. Nested deeper it's worse than empty: `{ foo: Promise.resolve({ bar: Promise.resolve({ invalid() {} }) }) }` reports `.invalid`, which looks like a real path and isnt one.

`keys` is pushed and popped as the synchronous walk goes, and a promises contents get flattened in a callback that only runs once that walk has finished unwinding it. So this captures the path at the thenable and puts it back for the length of the callback.

Without the `try/finally` a sibling promise that throws first leaves its keys on the array, and `{ a: <slow promise of a function>, b: Promise.resolve(() => {}) }` reports `.b.a` insted of `.a`.

pr.title: fix(parse): validate indices before dereferencing malformed payloads
pr.body:
### Problem

`parse` has two guards whose job is to reject malformed payloads with a clear error, but both dereference `values` *before* validating the index they were handed. When the index is not a valid one, the lookup yields `undefined` (or `null`), the `[0]` access on it throws a raw `TypeError`, and the guard never runs.

On `main`:

```js
parse('[["Uint8Array",9,0,1]]')      // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')
parse('[["Uint8Array",-1,0,1]]')     // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')
parse('[["Uint8Array",1,0,1],null]') // TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '0')
parse('[["DataView",4,0,1]]')        // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')
parse('[["Object",1],null]')         // TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '0')
```

All five are expected to be `Invalid data` / `Invalid input` — the messages the surrounding code already throws for the other malformed shapes in the same `switch`. Callers that distinguish "this input is not devalue output" from "devalue itself broke" currently cannot, since the failure surfaces as an internal `TypeError` about property access.

Two related holes in the same guards:

- `typeof null === 'object'` is why `["Object", <index of null>]` slips through the boxed-primitive check instead of being rejected.
- `["Object", -1]` (the `UNDEFINED` sentinel) boxes `undefined`, producing a plain `{}` — not a value `stringify` can emit.

### Fix

Validate the index before using it as a lookup in both guards, reject `null` explicitly, and restrict the boxed-primitive path to the sentinels `stringify` actually emits for boxed numbers (`NAN`, `POSITIVE_INFINITY`, `NEGATIVE_INFINITY`, `NEGATIVE_ZERO`).

This is a behavior change only for input that already failed — every one of these payloads threw before, just with the wrong error. No valid payload changes: I checked round-trips for `new Number(1)`, `new Number(NaN)`, `new Number(-0)`, `new Number(±Infinity)`, `new String`, `new Boolean` and `Object(10n)`, all of which still box correctly (`Object.is` on the unboxed value holds, including `-0`).

### Tests

Added 9 cases to the existing `invalid` table covering the typed-array/DataView index (out-of-bounds, negative, `null`, non-numeric), the DataView path, and the boxed-primitive index (`null`, out-of-bounds, non-numeric, unboxable sentinel).

`pnpm test`: **814 passed, 0 failed**. Reverting `src/parse.js` while keeping the tests fails 7 of them with exactly the raw `TypeError`s above, so they pin the fix rather than the current behavior.

pr.title: fix(format): honor an explicit indent of `0` or `""` on parsed values
pr.body:
### The problem

`stringifyJSON`, `stringifyJSONC` and `stringifyJSON5` accept an `indent` option, and `0` / `""` are the documented way to ask for minified output — that is what `JSON.stringify(value, null, 0)` does.

It works on a plain object but is silently ignored on a value that came from `parse*`, which is the main way values enter confbox:

```js
import { parseJSON, stringifyJSON } from "confbox";

const text = '{\n    "a": 1,\n    "b": { "c": 2 }\n}';

stringifyJSON({ a: 1, b: { c: 2 } }, { indent: 0 });
// '{"a":1,"b":{"c":2}}'          ← minified, as asked

stringifyJSON(parseJSON(text), { indent: 0 });
// '{\n    "a": 1,\n    "b": {\n        "c": 2\n    }\n}'   ← option ignored
```

### Cause

`getFormat` picks the indentation with `||`:

```ts
const indent = opts?.indent || detectIndent(format.sample || "").indent;
```

`0` and `""` are falsy, so an explicit request to minify falls through to the detected indentation. The same function's early return already uses `??` (`opts?.indent ?? 2`), and `detectFormat` decides whether to keep a sample with `opts.indent === undefined`, so this line was the odd one out — the two branches of `getFormat` disagreed about what "no indent given" means.

### The change

One operator, `||` → `??`, so only `undefined` falls back to detection. Every other value, including `0` and `""`, is passed through to `JSON.stringify` / `json5.stringify` as written.

No behavior changes when `indent` is omitted: auto-detection is untouched, and that is asserted by the new tests as well as the existing suite.

`stringifyYAML` is unaffected — it calls `getFormat` with `preserveIndentation: false`, so there is no sample to detect from.

### Tests

A new `indent` block covers `0` and `""` across JSON, JSONC and JSON5, plus an assertion per format that omitting `indent` still auto-detects. Reverting `src/_format.ts` fails exactly the 6 new minification cases and nothing else, so they pin the fix rather than restating existing behavior.

`pnpm test` → 37 passed, 1 skipped (the pre-existing `ini parse` skip). `pnpm lint` (oxlint + oxfmt) and `pnpm build` are clean.

No behavior changes when `indent` is omitted: auto-detection is untouched, and that is asserted by the new tests as well as the existing suite.

`stringifyYAML` is unaffected — it calls `getFormat` with `preserveIndentation: false`, so there is no sample to detect from.

### Tests

A new `indent` block covers `0` and `""` across JSON, JSONC and JSON5, plus an assertion per format that omitting `indent` still auto-detects. Reverting `src/_format.ts` fails exactly the 6 new minification cases and nothing else, so they pin the fix rather than restating existing behavior.

pr.title: fix(yaml): use a non-zero indent when stringifying flat documents
pr.body:
### Problem

When `parseYAML` reads a document with no indented lines, such as `a: 1`, the detected indent is `""`. `stringifyYAML` passes its length, `0`, to `js-yaml`'s `dump`. Any nested value added to that object is then written at column 0, which changes the data when read back:

```js
const config = parseYAML("a: 1\n");
config.b = { c: [1, 2] };
stringifyYAML(config); // "a: 1\nb:\nc:\n- 1\n- 2\n"
parseYAML(stringifyYAML(config)); // { a: 1, b: null, c: [1, 2] }
```

### Change

`stringifyYAML` falls back to an indent of `2` when the detected indent is `0`. This is the same default `getFormat` uses for values that were not parsed. Detected non-zero indents and an explicit `indent` option behave as before.

### Tests

A new `yaml` test parses a flat document, adds a nested object and array, and checks both the output and that it parses back to the same data.

- Without the `src/yaml.ts` change: 1 failed, 28 passed, 1 skipped.
- With the change: 29 passed, 1 skipped. `pnpm test` (oxlint, oxfmt, tsc, vitest) and `pnpm build` pass.

pr.title: fix: don't keep callers alive through cached errors
pr.body:
### Problem

A failed lookup is cached as an `Error` in the resolve cache (the global one by default). V8 formats `error.stack` lazily: until it is first read, the error holds the raw call sites, and each one references its frame's receiver. With `try: true` nothing reads the stack, so the cache keeps the resolver's callers alive for as long as the cache lives, which for the global cache is the whole process.

This shows up in real builds. Nitro's externals plugin calls `resolveModuleURL(id, { try: true, … })` from Rollup's `resolveId` hook. In a Nuxt 4.5 app, 15 of those lookups fail (`vue/server-renderer/index.mjs` and `devalue/src/*.js`), and a heap snapshot taken during prerendering showed `__EXSOLVE_CACHE__ → Error → CallSiteInfo → PluginDriver → .graph → Graph`. That held the prerender bundle's whole Rollup module graph (~3 GB) through prerendering and the final server build.

### Fix

Read `error.stack` before caching, so V8 formats it into a string and drops the call sites. The same `Error` is still cached and re-thrown.

### Verification

- New test: resolves a missing module from inside a method, drops the object, forces GC and checks via `WeakRef` that it was collected. Fails on `main`, passes with the fix.
- `pnpm test` passes.
- Same change applied to the installed exsolve in that Nuxt app: live heap during prerender went from 4.3 GB to 1.2 GB.

pr.title: perf: use `throwIfNoEntry: false` in `tryStatSync`
pr.body:
`tryStatSync` wraps `statSync` in try/catch, so every missing path throws an `ENOENT` error with a stack trace. Resolution checks many missing paths, so one failed lookup can throw thousands of times.

This passes `throwIfNoEntry: false`, like `fileExists` in the same file does. The try/catch stays for other errors.

Nitro 2 hits this once per server chunk. In a 12-layer Nuxt 4 app, a failed lookup went from about 28 ms to 13 ms, and the Nitro step from about 62 s to 42 s. The build output is the same.

Repro, with 640 throws per lookup before and 0 after: https://github.com/onmax/repros/tree/repro/exsolve-stat-throw

```sh
git clone --branch repro/exsolve-stat-throw https://github.com/onmax/repros.git
cd repros
for d in exsolve-stat-throw exsolve-stat-throw-fix; do (cd $d && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm verify); done
```

pr.title: fix: handle symlinked parents, `..`, `try` and empty input for absolute paths
pr.body:
Resolves #76

Fixes the edge cases in the absolute-path fast path of `resolveModuleURL` and in `_parseInput`, on top of `preserveSymlinks` (#72) and the cache fix (#77, 4cb62ee). All five items reproduced before the fix.

### 1. Symlinked parent directories

The fast path now uses `statSync` in both modes. In default mode, an absolute file input returns `realpathSync(absolutePath)` with the input's `search`/`hash` kept. With `preserveSymlinks`, the path is returned as-is. Before, default mode used `lstatSync`, which only caught a symlink in the last path segment; that case fell through to `finalizeResolution`.

A file reached through a symlinked directory (pnpm `node_modules/pkg -> store/pkg`, macOS `/var` -> `/private/var`) now resolves to the same URL as the relative/bare form and Node's `import.meta.resolve`. A last-segment symlink now resolves directly in the fast path instead of going through the slow path.

**Cost (default mode, cache miss only):** the JS `realpathSync` does one `lstat` per path segment, so an uncached absolute file costs `1 + depth` syscalls instead of 1. There is no cheaper way to tell whether any parent segment is a symlink.
- `finalizeResolution` already does the same `stat` + `realpathSync` for every relative/bare resolution, and Node does it for every import.
- The result is cached by default. Preserve mode stays at one `statSync`.
- On a ~11-segment path with `cache: false`: ~3.3µs on main, ~22µs on this PR, and ~29µs for an uncached relative resolution.

`realpathSync.native` would be about 2x cheaper. I left it out on purpose: it can return a different string than the JS `realpathSync` used by `finalizeResolution` (macOS case correction, Windows subst/network drives). That would bring back the "two IDs for one module" problem this item is about.

### 2. `..` after a symlinked directory

Absolute path strings are now normalized the same way `pathToFileURL` normalizes them: `.`/`..` segments are resolved and a trailing separator is kept. The path that is stat'ed is therefore the path that is returned. Without this, `lnk/../x.mjs` resolves through the symlink target in preserve mode. In default mode the `realpathSync` from fix 1 happens to mask it.

On Windows, `\\?\` long-path inputs still go through `fileURLToPath(pathToFileURL(…))`, which drops the prefix like the returned URL does. A Windows-only test covers this.

**Cache hits:** the URL for an absolute path string is now built only on a cache miss, and the cache key is the normalized path. Path strings have no search/hash, and `file:` inputs are still keyed on `url.href`. A cache hit for an absolute path string now costs ~1.24µs, compared with ~1.95µs on main.

### 3. `try: true` in the fast-path `catch`

Errors other than `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` (`ELOOP`, `EACCES`, `ENAMETOOLONG`, ...) are still cached, but now return `undefined` when `try` is set. Before, the first call threw and the second, served from the cache, returned `undefined`.

Since default mode now uses `statSync`, a self-looping symlink without `try` throws `ELOOP` with `syscall: "stat"` in both modes. Before this PR, default mode reported `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` from the slow path, and preserve mode already threw `ELOOP`. The #77 test that asserted `syscall: "lstat"` is updated accordingly.

### 4. Empty input

`""` returns `undefined` with `try`, otherwise it throws `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, like Node's `import.meta.resolve("")`. Before, it threw a `TypeError`.

The cache key and the search target both used `specifier || url.href`, which read `href` from an undefined `url`. Both now use `absolutePath` to tell absolute inputs apart.

### 5. Absolute misses probed once per `from` base

Absolute inputs now search with `bases = [url]`. `from` is only normalized for the error message, which is unchanged. Example: 3 non-existent string `from` entries plus `extensions: [".mjs"]` went from 15 `statSync` calls to 6.

### Also fixed

- **Suffixes/extensions after search/hash (from review):** they used to be appended after an absolute URL's `?query#hash`, so `file:///…/hello?x=1` with `extensions: [".mjs"]` probed `hello?x=1.mjs`. Absolute inputs are now probed without search/hash, which is restored on the result. Main had the same bug. Relative specifiers with a query are unchanged.
- **Trailing separator on Windows:** a file path with a trailing separator is no longer accepted by the fast path. Windows `stat` ignores a trailing separator, which is the same issue as 8864bce. The result now matches `finalizeResolution`, which reports not found, in both modes.

### Tests

- New fixture: `test/fixture/links/foo -> ../foo`, a git symlink like `hello.link.mjs`. It sits in a subdirectory so that `links/foo/..` (the fixture dir, followed through the symlink) differs from the textual parent (`links/`), which item 2 needs.
- `test/resolve.test.ts` covers, in both modes where relevant:
  - items 1 and 2;
  - item 3 with `ENAMETOOLONG`, plus `ELOOP` from a self-loop symlink created in a temp dir (skipped on Windows);
  - item 4;
  - search/hash with suffixes and extensions;
  - trailing-slash inputs.
- Item 5 lives in `test/resolve-probes.test.ts`, which already wraps `statSync`; the test now counts probes there.
- Each fix makes a test fail when reverted. The exception is the trailing-slash test, which only catches a regression on Windows CI: POSIX `stat` already fails with `ENOTDIR`.

issue_texts.76:
Absolute path fast path: symlinked parents, `..` segments, `try` and empty input

Follow-up from the review of #72. The absolute-path fast path in `resolveModuleURL` (`src/resolve.ts`) and `_parseInput` have several edge cases that can be fixed together in one PR. All of these reproduce with #72 applied.

### 1. Symlinked parent directories are not resolved

The fast path uses `lstatSync`, so only a symlink in the **last** path component is resolved. A regular file reached through a symlinked directory is returned as-is in both modes, so `preserveSymlinks` has no effect on it.

```
proj/node_modules/pkg -> ../../store/pkg
```

```js
resolveModuleURL("/…/proj/node_modules/pkg/index.mjs");
// => file:///…/proj/node_modules/pkg/index.mjs
```

Resolving the bare `pkg` from `proj/src/`, the relative form, and Node's `import.meta.resolve` all return `store/pkg/index.mjs`. A bundler keying on the returned string gets two IDs for one module (pnpm layouts, macOS `/var` -> `/private/var` under `os.tmpdir()`).

Possible fix: in default mode, return `realpathSync` of the file from the fast path (keeping `search`/`hash`), or skip the fast return when the path is not already canonical.

### 2. `..` after a symlinked directory returns a path that doesn't exist

`lstatSync` lets the kernel follow the symlink before applying `..`, but the returned URL comes from `pathToFileURL`, which collapses `..` as text.

```
lnk -> deep/nested/real
deep/nested/x.mjs   (no x.mjs next to lnk)
```

```js
resolveModuleURL("<abs>/lnk/../x.mjs", { try: true });
// => file:///<abs>/x.mjs   (does not exist)
```

The relative form and Node's `import()` reject this input. Fix: `absolutePath: fileURLToPath(url)` in `_parseInput`, so the path that is checked is the path that is returned.

### 3. The fast-path `catch` ignores `try: true`

Every error except `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` is cached and rethrown, even with `try: true`. The cache-hit branch does honor `try`, so the first call throws and the second returns `undefined`.

```js
// loop.mjs -> loop.mjs
resolveModuleURL(abs, { try: true, preserveSymlinks: true }); // throws ELOOP
resolveModuleURL(abs, { try: true, preserveSymlinks: true }); // undefined (from cache)
```

`EACCES` (e.g. a `chmod 000` parent directory) behaves the same way in both modes. Fix: return `undefined` in that `catch` when `options.try` is set.

### 4. Empty input throws a TypeError, even with `try: true`

```js
resolveModuleURL("", { try: true });
// TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'href')
```

`specifier || url.href` reads `href` from an undefined `url`. Expected: `undefined` with `try`, otherwise `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (as Node's `import.meta.resolve('')` throws).

### 5. Absolute misses are probed once per `from` base

When an absolute input misses the fast path, each probe is an absolute `file:` URL whose result doesn't depend on the base. The slow path still normalizes every `from` entry (a `statSync` each) and repeats every suffix/extension probe per base. With 3 string `from` entries and 2 extensions that is 9 probes instead of 3.

Fix: `const bases = absolutePath ? [url] : _normalizeBases(options?.from)`, normalizing `from` only for the error message.

### Tests

Current fixtures only use a symlink in the last path component. A fixture such as `test/fixture/link-dir -> foo`, with an absolute path under it asserted in both `preserveSymlinks` modes, would cover 1 and guard the fast path.

Fix: `const bases = absolutePath ? [url] : _normalizeBases(options?.from)`, normalizing `from` only for the error message.

### Tests

Current fixtures only use a symlink in the last path component. A fixture such as `test/fixture/link-dir -> foo`, with an absolute path under it asserted in both `preserveSymlinks` modes, would cover 1 and guard the fast path.
